title: Mortgage squeeze hits Tasmanians after repeated rate rises
text:
Alex Gill and her partner built their family home in Tasmania's south three years ago.

Like a lot of new builds, it ended up costing the family more than they'd budgeted for.

The latest interest rate rise will make things tighter for the family of four.

Tasmanian homeowner Alex Gill says the repeated interest rate rises are definitely having an impact. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6pc The Reserve Bank increases interest rates to 4.6 per cent in its fourth rate rise this year.

Ms Gill said she may have to consider increasing her part-time working hours.

And while on average Tasmania's wages are on average lower than other states, Ms Gill said the family have no plans to move interstate.

"We're just going to have to make it work because we love being here, we love Tasmania," she said.

But, if interest rates continue to climb, the family may need to consider more drastic action.

"It definitely makes us think about maybe selling in the future and not staying in the home that we're in because things are getting up there," she said.

Tasmanian homeowner Ella Tenni is in the process of buying and selling at the moment, and says the interest rate rise does add some uncertainty into the mix. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Ella Tenni, who also lives in Southern Tasmania, is weighing up what the interest rate rise will mean for her family.

"We're in the process of selling and buying at the moment," Ms Tenni said.

"So I did have a bit of a pause, maybe feeling a bit worried about that, but in the scheme of things we're in a position that we'll be able to absorb it."

She said she sometimes worries about further interest rate rises.

"But then I do sometimes put my head in the sand and try not to think about it."

The average new loan size for Tasmania at the start of the year was $505,000. (ABC News: Jacinta Bos )

Lower wages, big mortgages

Consumer research company Canstar has looked at what impact the 0.25 per cent cash rate hike will have on monthly mortgage repayments.

What's impacted in the RBA rate hike While the RBA's decisions are most felt through mortgage repayments, their impact extends well beyond home loans.

For someone who took out the average new loan size for Tasmania at the start of the year of $505,000, the rate hike will translate into an increase to their minimum monthly repayments of $81.

That's based on a 30-year loan at a variable rate of 5.50 per cent.

"While plenty of households might be able to handle this kind of increase in isolation, across what has now been four cash rate hikes in 2026, that same borrower has seen their monthly repayments rise by a total of $322," Canstar's Sally Tindall said.

Sally Tindall says the repeat rate rises are having a compounding impact on households across the country. (Supplied: CANSTAR)

" That's not a one-off expense. That's how much extra they have to pay the bank every month for the foreseeable future. "

On top of that, Tasmania's wages are the lowest in the country.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, Tasmania's average weekly earnings are $1846.30 — compared with a national figure of $2083.70.

The latest figures from Cotality show the median property value in Hobart is over $750 000, while still cheaper than most states and territories, it has been on the rise since the pandemic.

Businesses bracing for belt-tightening

Andrew Turner says the topic of inflation and rate rises is on the minds of customers and staff alike. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Andrew Turner owns a café and brewery in Burnie.

He said every time interest rates rise, there's a change in sentiment among his customers.

"I don't know if we get a huge drop in revenue, but it's definitely something everyone is talking about," he said.

Andrew Turner says he's expecting customers to keep tightening their belt, due to the cost of living. (ABC Northern Tasmania: Monte Bovill)

"Even our staff are talking about now having issues affording their homes."

" I think in north-west Tasmania, because our general mortgage rates aren't as high as some of the big cities, we're still a little bit protected. "

He said he's expecting future rate rises will start to affect customer spending and his business won't be in a position to drop prices.

"All of our costs have gone through the roof as well, and now with the surcharge ban we're looking at absorbing a significant cost as a part of that."

Tips for mortgage holders and advice for government

Canstar's Sally Tindall said it was time the government considered looking at a different way to manage inflation, other than the RBA lifting interest rates.

She said in the last nine months inflation reduction had stalled but at the same time borrowers and renters are paying more.

The Reserve Bank of Australia this week lifted interest rates to the highest level in 15 years. (ABC News: Kylie Silvester)

"But yet savings rates go up for people who are mortgage-free," she said.

"Some people need that extra interest; there's no doubt about it.

" But it does seem crazy that the screws get tighter for, you know, a cohort of borrowers and renters and then the screws get a little bit looser for a different cohort. "

RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6pc The Reserve Bank increases interest rates to 4.6 per cent in its fourth rate rise this year.

Her advice to borrowers is "take a deep breath and get planning".

She said even though rates are on the way up, it's still a good time to find a better home loan deal.

"We've seen a large number of lenders actually cut variable rates — yes, cut.

" In a sea of hikes, we're seeing them cut them, but only for new customers. "

title: One EV sold every 100 seconds as Australia catches up to the world
text:
An electric car is being sold every 100 seconds in Australia, but there is still a long road ahead to decarbonise the country's transport sector, according to the Electric Vehicle Council.

The 10th anniversary edition of the annual State of Electric Vehicles Report shows how EVs have become mainstream within a decade, making up one in four new cars sold.

Sales have more than doubled within a year and last month, EVs outsold petrol and diesel cars for the first time.

"EVs are being taken up as a cost of living measure by households across Australia," Julie Delvecchio, CEO of the Electric Vehicle Council, said.

Owning an EV is no longer a luxury reserved for well-heeled inner-city dwellers as electric cars come close to price parity with petrol versions. Some are now selling for under $20,000.

Electric cars are no longer more expensive than petrol cars, with some models selling under $20,000. (Facebook: Electric Vehicle Council)

This year's sales boom is being driven by suburban commuters, with the highest EV uptake in Tarneit, about 30 kilometres west of Melbourne.

"It's very much an average Australian suburb with people who have mortgages in the six to seven hundred thousands," Aman Gaur, the EVC's Head of Legal, Policy and Advocacy, said.

"They rely on their cars, they do not have access to three forms of public transport outside their front door, and for them, the sensible economic choice is to get into an EV."

Australians now have access to nearly 200 electric models, and incentives such as the fringe benefit tax exemption have helped to drive uptake.

The beginning of the conflict with Iran in February and the subsequent disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has seen fuel prices to surge this year, helping to further push the number of EVs currently on the road to more than 600,000.

"Australia is an island at the end of a long fuel supply chain, holding weeks' worth of reserves and importing almost all of its fuel," the Electric Vehicle Council (EVC) report said.

"Every car that plugs in instead of filling up is a permanent upgrade to our energy security."

Long road to meet climate goals

While 2026 may well become a turning point for passenger EVs, reaching Australia's climate targets will require a revolution in the national fleet.

There are about 21 million cars on Australian roads, and EVs make up just 3 per cent compared to internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles.

"While the doubling of EV uptake over the last year is great news, Australia needs to maintain this momentum to be on track to reach its climate targets," Helen Rowe, the transport lead at the Monash University's Climateworks Centre, said.

The EVC report notes that Australia's EV uptake is not on track to meet the emission reduction targets of 43 per cent below 2005 levels by 2030, and 62 to 70 per cent by 2035.

"That 2035 target requires 5 million battery electric cars on the road by the middle of the next decade—a significant increase in pace from the current trajectory," the EVC's report said.

All consumers to pay for EV chargers A bitter fight is brewing between EV charging companies and poles-and-wires companies, and now a regulator has weighed in.

The other hurdle is charging infrastructure; it's increasing, but not quite keeping pace, according to the EVC's Aman Gaur.

"We do need to have a coordinated charging plan that will help Australians have confidence that they can get out onto the roads and charge either their car or their truck or their van," he said.

Addicted to diesel

Per capita, Australia uses more diesel than the US, China and Saudi Arabia.

And the biggest user of diesel is the transport and freight sector, which has barely started to electrify.

That's not because there are no electric trucks; while still more expensive, there are a growing number of options.

"China, the undisputed leader on truck electrification, saw monthly sales breach 50 per cent in December 2025 and already appears advanced in meeting its new 2030 target for 40 per cent heavy electric truck sales," The EVC report said.

Most freight operators in Australia are small businesses, running on very tight margins, and according to the EVC's Aman Gaur, the cost of switching to electric trucks was still prohibitive.

"There aren't enough financial incentives to get small mum and dad operators to make the switch to electric, which means that Australia is still importing diesel and our economy is still reliant on those imports," he said.

The EVC report called Australia a "global laggard" when it came to adopting electric trucks, with heavy vehicle rules such as road weight limits "complex and notoriously difficult to reform."

"With almost zero policy support and no dedicated charging infrastructure to speak of, electric trucks are yet to hit even 1 per cent of total truck sales.

"This contrasts with European markets and New Zealand, where strong freight electrification policies are moving heavy EVs beyond the 'early adopter' cohort to everyday trucking fleets.

"Electrifying Australia's heavy freight vehicles is the biggest unseized opportunity in Australia's energy transition."

title: Planning decision to extend life of mega coal mine saves 1,500 jobs
text:
An estimated 1,500 jobs have been saved after the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) handed down its ruling on the future of a major coal mine near Singleton in the New South Wales Hunter Valley.

The IPC today approved plans that will allow Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) to continue mining at the site until 2045, extracting an estimated 429 million tonnes of coal across its North and South sites.

In April 2025, the mine was given a last-minute extension, which allowed it to continue operating until December this year.

HVO told IPC hearings in July that the mine employed more than 1,500 people, engaged more than 800 suppliers and injected more than $1 billion a year into the economy.

But environmentalists argued the extension would put the NSW government's ability to reach its net-zero targets in jeopardy.

The proposal had backing from Premier Chris Minns and Natural Resources Minister Courtney Houssos, as well as the NSW Coalition.

"Those 1,500 jobs are such a key part of the state's economy, but particularly here in the Hunter Valley," Ms Houssos told ABC Upper Hunter ahead of today's decision.

"We've got legislated net-zero emissions targets and we will adhere to those, but we also understand the important role that coal mining has particularly for the Hunter Valley, but for our entire state's economy," she said.

More than 10,000 public submissions were made to the IPC during its deliberations, with about 60 per cent supporting the project.

The Independent Planning Commission has released its decision on the future of Hunter Valley Operations. (ABC 730)

The IPC released a statement acknowledging the emission of 809 megatonnes (Mt) of greenhouse gases from the mining operations and coal combustion overseas would contribute to climate change impacts across the Hunter, NSW and globally.

But it said those impacts were balanced against the "significant employment, business, social and economic benefits of the mine extension".

The approval comes with conditions, including implementing measures to limit coal exports to jurisdictions that have policies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions consistent with the Paris Agreement, maximising the use of renewable energy at the mine, and purchasing additional carbon offsets.

Georgina Woods from the Lock the Gate Alliance. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

Lock The Gate Alliance national coordinator Georgina Woods said the IPC decision was a "crossroads moment for the Hunter and NSW".

"We are right on this knife edge of dangerous levels of global warming, but obviously also too little has been done to prepare the Hunter region for the closure of mines," she said.

"Every single year, greenhouse gas pollution resulting from this mine will wipe out all the efforts that everyone in Australia and NSW is making to reduce our own pollution.

"That's how stark it is."

Ms Woods said the decision would "unwind all of our good work".

"It's [now] pretty much impossible to avoid that dangerous level of 1.5 degrees of warming, and that will have profound consequences," she said.

" Lost income, lost jobs, lost food production, lost culture, lost lives and livelihoods. "

HVO has released a statement saying the decision brought it "one step closer to long-term certainty".

"HVO still needs to secure a critical federal government environmental approval by the end of December 2026 to continue operations," it said.

"We will continue to engage with the National Environmental Protection Agency to secure the final approval needed to protect 1,500 regional jobs and deliver economic certainty and stability for the Hunter region."

title: Minister says Perth barracks sale will not mean bulldozers for heritage sites
text:
The planned sale of Perth's Irwin and Leeuwin barracks will free up land in highly desirable suburbs but developers will not have free rein to bulldoze the sites for housing, defence minister Richard Marles has said.

Speaking to Nadia Mitsopoulos on 102.5 ABC Perth, Mr Marles also said the sales were still some way off and would not proceed until the cadets and army reservists who currently use the sites had transitioned to an alternative site.

"This whole exercise is making sure that our Defence estate is more fit for purpose for what Defence does," he said.

"In respect of [Leeuwin and Irwin barracks], what we are thinking mostly about is both reserves and cadets here in Perth and making sure that the outcome here … is better sites.

"That it is ultimately a better outcome for our reservists and for our cadets.

"A lot of the activity that is undertaken by cadets and reserves now, and this would include in respect of these two sites, is happening on old sites which are really not that fit for purpose for what they're doing."

Mr Marles also said the Defence department was working closely with the WA RSL branch to consult on the move of some activity to Palmer Barracks in South Guildford.

Both Irwin and Leeuwin barracks occupy substantial amounts of land in highly desirable residential areas. Irwin Barracks covers 61.5 hectares in the heart of Perth's affluent western suburbs, while Leeuwin occupies 14 hectares on the Swan riverfront at East Fremantle.

Both sites require some remediation and preparation before they will be transferred to the Department of Finance, which will handle the sale.

While he could not say whether any expressions of interest had been received or how much the sites may be worth, Mr Marles said both sites were protected by heritage overlays, which would limit how far they could be developed.

"They are protected by law and they will be protected by law," he said.

"None of these sites are going to be bulldozed.

"In fact, I think what will happen with a lot of these heritage sites is that they will be opened up to the public much more and people will be able to enjoy them."

title: The backstory of this year's Fat Bear Week winner
text:
A new champion has been crowned in this year's edition of Fat Bear Week.

The annual online poll, which showcases brown bears in Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve, ended with a battle between two of the region's most titanic residents.

If you're unfamiliar with the popularity contest, or missed this year's festivities, our Fat Bear Week group chat will get you up to speed.

D Dannielle Maguire Geez, I'm hearing a lot of chatter about Fat Bear Week. What did I miss?!

E Elissa Fitzgerald 89 Backpack was this year's heavyweight champ. I think he was a favourite among the live-stream viewers.

G Georgie Hewson I just checked the final tally: 89 Backpack got about 103,000 votes while 910 had about 98,000. A pretty close result!

D Dannielle Maguire Who? Why is he called Backpack?

E Elissa Fitzgerald 89 Backpack's name is a reference to how he would climb onto his mother's back when swimming in the river. His mother Holly won Fat Bear Week in 2019. About 20 years old, he's known for being a calm fella. While most adult male bears show aggression to their competitors, Backpack uses a quiet strength to gain access to his favourite fishing spots.

G Georgie Hewson Nepo baby!

E Elissa Fitzgerald Technically both finalists are nepo babies. 910's mother, 409 Beadnose, won Fat Bear Week in 2015 and 2018.

G Georgie Hewson Check out the before-and-after photos of the adults!

Loading

D Dannielle Maguire As a Paddington super fan, I'm thrilled to see all this bear chat but I don't really get what Fat Bear Week is.

G Georgie Hewson It's like a popularity contest for a group of bears living in this one specific national park in Alaska.

E Elissa Fitzgerald It was started by a fellow bear enthusiast! Back in 2012, cameras were installed throughout the park so people could watch live streams of the bears fishing for salmon. And people got right into it. It had a huge following.

D Dannielle Maguire Sounds like a soothing watch!

E Elissa Fitzgerald Super relaxing. One year, a viewer posted a before-and-after comparison of how much one of the bears had beefed up. This blew up on social media and eventually led to park rangers capitalising on the fan interest and starting up the week-long comp.

G Georgie Hewson I think it's safe to say we all appreciate them for kick-starting one of the most wholesome events on the internet calendar.

D Dannielle Maguire So it's an online vote?

G Georgie Hewson Yep, and people all over the world vote for their favourite bears.

D Dannielle Maguire So what's it got to do with the bears beefing up?

E Elissa Fitzgerald The bears are bulking up so they can survive off their fat stores when they hibernate for winter. They're basically prepping for a months-long famine.

D Dannielle Maguire Ohhh yeah, it's spring here, which means it's autumn in the northern hemisphere. How much do you reckon you need to eat before hibernation?

G Georgie Hewson I saw Katmai rangers saying the bears can eat more than 30 salmon a day. I can't imagine having the same meal every day 🥴

E Elissa Fitzgerald I've just done the maths on that. With salmon about 4,500 calories a pop, it means these ursine bodybuilders have a typical daily intake of about 135,000 calories! And I thought my bulking seasons were gnarly …

D Dannielle Maguire That's a lot of food! So how does this competition work? How does a bear win?

E Elissa Fitzgerald They have knockout rounds, like the World Cup. Here's how it looked this year:

The voting system is structured a bit like the World Cup tournament. (Explore.org)

G Georgie Hewson People are told to vote for "the bear you believe best exemplifies fatness and success in brown bears".

D Dannielle Maguire So it's not about kilos, but more the vibe of the thing?

E Elissa Fitzgerald Yeah, pretty much.

D Dannielle Maguire Who were you lot wanting to win? I didn't mind that 164 Bucky fella …

E Elissa Fitzgerald I stuck with the reigning champ, 32 Chunk. He copped a broken jaw last year and learned to adapt to his disability. Before that, he had been a Fat Bear Week runner-up four times, so I was happy to see the corpulent king defending his title. Too bad Bucky knocked him out in the first round!

G Georgie Hewson I liked 131 Marshmallow. She had the cutest name. Apparently, this year she got "proportionally fatter than she has ever been". I have to root for a woman in a male-dominated field. Go girl!

E Elissa Fitzgerald Speaking of cute, I loved seeing the family unit entries this year.

D Dannielle Maguire Was that a new thing?

G Georgie Hewson Yes! We used to get the mini tournament, Fat Bear Week Junior, for the chubby cubbies, but that was scrapped. They competed with their mums in the big leagues this year 🥺

E Elissa Fitzgerald One of the family units was 901 and her cub. During the season, 901 Jr was caught on the live stream with porcupine quills in its paw. Hopefully it learned an important lesson about playing with wildlife!

D Dannielle Maguire So, what was so good about this year's winner? Why do you reckon he won?

E Elissa Fitzgerald Riding on his mother's back is a pretty cute anecdote, and he sounds like a sweetheart. The comp's organisers said: "Backpack's quiet toughness has allowed him to find his niche alongside the biggest bears at Brooks River". Awww!

G Georgie Hewson Plus, he's a bit of an underdog. He had a leg injury in when he was little and didn't put on much weight that summer, so people were wondering if he would survive. Now look at him!

D Dannielle Maguire Rightio, so what's the next animal-related, kind-of-weird-but-actually-really-quite-sweet internet event I should mark my calendar for?

E Elissa Fitzgerald The Fish Doorbell's coming back in March!

D Dannielle Maguire Excuse me?

title: November rate rise less likely with inflation data lower than expected
text:
The odds of the Reserve Bank lifting interest rates in November have fallen sharply after the latest consumer price index (CPI) came in lower than expected.

Annual headline inflation jumped to 4 per cent in August, up from 3.5 per cent in July, according to the Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

It was slightly lower than the 4.1 per cent inflation that economists were predicting ahead of the official numbers being released.

But trimmed mean inflation, the RBA's preferred measure of underlying inflation, remained steady at 3.6 per cent for the third month in a row.

The ABS numbers show that consumer prices are still rising, but at a slower rate than was expected.

The news comes a day after the central bank lifted interest rates for the fourth time this year, to their highest level in 15 years, to try to drag inflation down and stop high inflation becoming embedded in Australia's economy.

Money markets are now betting the RBA will likely keep rates on hold at its next meeting in early November. The odds of a rate hike fell to around 20 per cent, according to market data from LSEG.

Despite that, Westpac's chief economist Luci Ellis is predicting the RBA will lift rates again in a couple of months, "absent a lasting resolution of the Middle East conflict beforehand, or some other event that significantly lowers the outlook for energy-related costs in Australia".

Housing and fuel prices surge

Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation last month, reflecting rising costs for new dwellings and electricity.

RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6pc The Reserve Bank increases interest rates to 4.6 per cent in its fourth rate rise this year.

"New dwelling prices rose 5.4 per cent in the 12 months to August as builders passed on higher costs for materials and labour," Rachael McCririck, ABS head of price statistics, said.

Transport was the second-largest contributor to annual inflation, due to higher automotive fuel prices.

"On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 14.8 per cent in August, compared to a rise of 7.5 per cent in July," Ms McCririck said.

"This was driven by higher world oil prices and the unwinding of the remainder of the federal government's fuel excise relief measures in August."

RBA wants underlying inflation lower

In a press conference on Tuesday, RBA governor Michele Bullock said underlying inflation had been sitting around 3.5 per cent for the last six months and the RBA wanted to drag it down.

"That's telling us what's happened in the past," she said.

'Pressures bearing down' on rates Why is Australia stuck in an inflation problem that has sent interest rates to 15-year highs?

"We can't influence that. That's what happened. So we now need to make sure that we have financial conditions tight enough to try to bring that down.

"We raised interest rates three times earlier this year, a lot of that effect is still to flow through … What we are predicting, what is the hope here, is that [four] interest rate increases will bring things down.

"Will it be enough? I don't know," she said.

Interest rates are at a 15-year high. Tell us how this will impact your livelihood or business here.

Unemployment and interest rates

KPMG chief economist Brendan Rynne said today's inflation data validated the RBA's decision to lift interest rates on Tuesday.

"Today's inflation print shows a stubbornness that requires more drastic policy action, importantly both monetary and fiscal policy working together, in order to bring inflation back down to the RBA mid-point target of 2.5 per cent," he said.

Rate rise looking likely All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders believe the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates next week and governor Michele Bullock did nothing to dissuade them during a speech in Sydney.

He also backed the argument that Australia needed higher unemployment to drag inflation down.

"Much has been spoken this week about the need for the labour market to cool further to assist in the taming of inflation, with the RBA governor suggesting the unemployment rate may need to move to within the 5 per cent band in order for domestic demand to slow sufficiently enough to retard inflation," he said.

"Today's CPI data reinforces this policy target as it shows the capital city with the lowest inflation outcome, Melbourne (3.5 per cent) is also the one with the highest unemployment rate (5.2 per cent)."

EY senior economist Paula Gadsby said that on a six-month annualised measure, trimmed mean inflation was running at 3.9 per cent in August, which was higher than the 12-month measure of 3.6 per cent.

She said that underscored the challenge the Reserve Bank faced.

"We expect the board may need to raise interest rates again before the end of the year if, as we expect, inflation momentum fails to moderate," she said.

Concerns about higher unemployment

But others have raised concerns about using higher unemployment to drag inflation down.

Earlier this week, the Australian Council of Social Service (ACOSS) said the main causes of inflation at the moment sat on the supply side, which interest rates could not impact.

No evidence of a 'wage-price spiral' in Australia There is no evidence of runaway wage growth emerging in Australia, RBA board member Iain Ross says.

It said the Iran war, higher global fuel prices, climate change, energy prices, and housing supply shortages were all driving inflation higher.

It said on the demand side, there was little evidence that the economy was overheating.

"Inflation is not too high because unemployment is too low," it said.

"Real wages are below their pre-pandemic level and nominal wage growth is not accelerating. This did not happen even when unemployment reached a low point of 3.5 per cent after the pandemic in 2022.

"The unemployment rate now stands at 4.6 per cent and an extra 100,000 people now rely on JobSeeker Payment for more than a year," it said.

title: Neale set to join Magpies as Lions confirm exit
text:
Collingwood says it "looks forward" to Lachie Neale joining the club in 2027 after it was confirmed the three-time premiership player is leaving the Brisbane Lions.

Neale's departure was no secret, as he revealed he was going to miss the Lions "very much" when speaking immediately after Saturday's AFL grand final at the MCG.

This morning, the Lions confirmed the 33-year-old would leave the club as an unrestricted free agent.

"Lachie has been a great player for the Brisbane Lions, and we thank him for his incredible contribution over his eight seasons," Lions list manager Dom Ambrogio said in a club statement.

"We understand Lachie's reasons for wishing to explore free agency and we wish him all the best for the next chapter of his career."

Lions break Dockers' hearts The Brisbane Lions launch an incredible fightback late in the grand final to edge Fremantle by seven points and win a third consecutive premiership.

The Lions said they would "further celebrate and recognise Neale's contribution to the club in the coming days".

The Magpies did not waste time announcing Neale's intention to move south.

"Three-time premiership player and two-time Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale has decided to exercise his free agency rights with a move to Collingwood," a Magpies statement read.

"The club looks forward to welcoming him … when the AFL trade and free agency period commences on Friday."

The AFL is expected to confirm the suitable free agency compensation the Lions will receive during the trade and free agency period.

Speaking after the Lions clinched a third straight flag with a remarkable seven-point win over Fremantle in the grand final, Neale said he owed the club a lot.

"It doesn't feel real at the moment, but I'm sure it will sink in," Neale said on Saturday.

"I've absolutely loved my time at this footy club, they're an exceptional organisation from top to bottom and I can't thank them enough.

"It's been an incredible ride and the best eight years of my life."

Neale moved to the Lions from the Dockers at the end of the 2018 season.

He won his two Brownlow Medals (2020 and 2023) while playing 186 senior matches for the Lions.

Neale, a four-time All-Australian selection, played 135 matches for the Dockers between 2012-18.

title: Lone finalist for Brisbane Games stadium build announced
text:
A consortium has been selected as the only bidder to progress to the final stage of contract negotiations to build Brisbane's Olympic 63,000-seat stadium.

The site at Victoria Park was handed over to the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority in June, with earthworks underway ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Today, the joint venture of BESIX Watpac and John Holland has been announced as the sole builder to move to the next stage of contract negotiations.

Together the companies have delivered a host of stadiums including Lang Park, the Gabba, Melbourne's Docklands stadium and Penrith Stadium.

Earthworks are underway at the site for the new stadium. (Supplied: GIICA)

The contract process for the stadium started in October last year, with the consortium to now work with the stadium's design team to finalise details and construction methodology.

GIICA chief executive Simon Crooks said the early contract process had been comprehensive.

"We are satisfied that the process has delivered the best possible contractor for this second and final phase," Mr Crooks said.

The stadium is slated to cost about $3.6 billion, and forms part of the $7.1 billion infrastructure plan for the 2032 Games.

Contracts are set to be finalised in the new year, with construction to begin in 2027.

After the Games, the stadium is set to become the home ground for the Brisbane Lions AFL team and cricket's Brisbane Heat and Queensland Bulls.

'No cost blowouts'

Olympics Minister Tim Mander said while negotiations were continuing it was an important and exciting step forward.

"Now it is just a matter of trying to nut out the contracts so we can make sure there are no cost blowouts," he said.

When questioned about the cost of the stadium today, Premier David Crisafulli said he had never revealed the budget for individual projects, with details to be released when finished.

"It is about making sure we deliver the Games work within our agreements with the federal government for $7.1 billion and we are going to do that," he said.

"We respect people's money and I pride myself on that, but equally we are going to build something world-class.

"The negotiations that have been able to be done fill me with confidence that we will deliver it on time and on budget and all the progress that we are making is pointing in the right direction."

The site at Victoria Park was handed over to the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority in June. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Mr Crisafulli said there was more work to do before the contract was awarded.

"They have got to continue to show value for money and the ability to build a quality product for the state, that is important," he said.

Earlier this year, the government announced it had selected Australian firms Cox and Hassell to design the stadium, alongside Japanese group Azusa Sekkei.

The firms worked on Perth's Optus Stadium and redeveloped the Adelaide Oval and the MCG.

Victoria Park has been the target of ongoing protests against the development of the stadium, which peaked earlier this year with the arrest of several activists who opposed its construction at the site because of cultural and historic ties.

title: Finance presenter Alan Kohler retiring after three decades at ABC
text:
After a brilliant 31-year career as the ABC's finance guru, Alan Kohler has decided to hang up his boots at the end of the year.

With a successful career in print before moving to television, Kohler has been one of the most influential journalists Australia has ever produced, as a former editor of The Australian Financial Review (AFR) and The Age and as an incisive columnist on all affairs financial.

"I love the ABC, always have, even more so after I joined it," he told ABC staff in a statement.

" I find it very hard to imagine this wonderful place not being part of my life, but I'm 74 and it's time to spend more time with my family, including the six grandchildren. "

Alan Kohler (left) speaks with then-treasurer Paul Keating in 1984, during Kohler's time as editor of The Australian Financial Review. (Supplied)

Kohler joined the public broadcaster in 1995 as business and economics correspondent for the 7.30 Report and went on to host Inside Business.

For the past 24 years, he has been the lead 7pm News finance presenter, unravelling the mysteries of financial markets for the audience with a format all his own that has often begun with: "Now, here's an interesting graph."

ABC managing director Hugh Marks said Kohler had made an extraordinary contribution to the organisation and the nation.

Alan Kohler swapped the studio for the home office during COVID-19 pandemic. (Supplied)

"For decades, he has helped Australians make sense of complex issues with insight, clarity and a uniquely engaging style, always delivered with warmth, humour and that trademark cheeky grin.

"I can't thank Alan enough for everything he has given to the ABC and our audiences. While this marks the end of an incredible chapter, it is certainly not the end of Alan's contribution, just the beginning of a new one."

Kohler hosted Inside Business for many years. He currently writes a weekly column and hosts a podcast, That's Business, every Friday.

While he is a distinguished editor, Kohler's biggest impact on the nation has been as a communicator.

After several stints as the chanticleer columnist for the AFR, he joined The Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) and The Age as senior business columnist, working with your correspondent during my time as SMH business editor.

Alan Kohler worked as a journalist in Darwin during Cyclone Tracey. (Supplied)

A canny entrepreneur, he had by that stage already launched The Eureka Report and later left Fairfax Media when he added online news service Business Spectator to the mix.

Throughout his various incarnations, he has remained steadfastly loyal to the ABC and to his audience and is expected to continue his association with one-off specials.

title: Why Daniel Tupou is a Sydney Roosters grand final specialist
text:
The Roosters boast a galaxy of stars for Sunday's NRL decider against Newcastle, but veteran winger Daniel Tupou might be the only one who can call himself a grand final specialist.

Not that he ever would. The 35-year-old has for many years now been a firm believer that actions speak louder than words, and those actions demand his automatic inclusion in any discussion about an all-time Roosters XVII.

A win over the Knights will make Tupou, already the club's highest-ever tryscorer and only a few games shy of being their most capped player, the first Rooster to win four premierships with the club since the 1940s.

He's the only player to have appeared in all three grand final wins under coach Trent Robinson, although calling what Tupou has done merely "appearing" sells him short.

Back in 2013, in just his second year of first grade, Tupou went skywalking to score a spectacular try in the Tricolours' win over a Manly side containing future teammate Daly Cherry-Evans.

Tupou has been making his mark in grand finals for more than a decade. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Back then, Tupou was like so many of his teammates are now — young and hungry in his first grand final, with everything to prove.

"I can't remember much, to be honest it's a bit of a blur, it was such a long time ago. Most of these boys are where I was in 2013 — I was the same age then as Rob Toia is now," said Tupou.

"He's (Cherry-Evans) has never brought it up. I might not bring it up this week, not until after the game on Sunday at least."

That try was just the 17th of Tupou's career, and his 199th in the preliminary final win over the Dolphins is proof he can still fly.

But that and his calm demeanour are about the only things that are still the same after all this time, with Tupou himself having become one of the best wingers of the modern era in the years since.

His performances in the club's back-to-back premiership wins in 2018-19 are living proof of that transformation from skinny aerial specialist to a truly complete flanker.

In the first victory, a comprehensive win over Melbourne, he scored the opening try and worked like a dog from the backfield, running for the second-most metres of any Roosters player.

In the second, a 14-8 war with Canberra, he was unlucky not to become the first winger to win the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.

Tupou ran for a team-high 185 metres from 17 carries and saved several tries with perfect defensive decision-making before making the break and throwing the final pass for James Tedesco's premiership-winning score.

It's as good a game as a winger has ever played in a grand final, but when Tupou explains how he finds his best form on the season's biggest day, he makes it sound maddeningly simple.

"You have to stay calm and collected. Enjoy the week and the hype around it, enjoy the atmosphere once we hit the field but embrace the vibe, embrace the energy," said Tupou.

"There's a lot of stuff to tick off, but you have to enjoy every bit of it.

"Just stay present. Don't overthink, be where your feet are."

It's the advice he'll give the grand final rookies on Sunday, even though the Roosters have plenty of premiership experience on hand.

Victor Radley and James Tedesco both played in 2018-19, Nat Butcher and Angus Crichton were both there for the latter and Spencer Leniu won three titles with Penrith.

This Rooster has been the NRL's best forward in 2026 Fresh off another act of blunt-force artistry, there can be no doubt that Roosters prop Naufahu Whyte has been the best forward in the NRL in 2026.

But given 15 of the 22 players named on Tuesday have yet to play in a grand final, they have a fair share of first-timers.

None could ask for a better example of how to make the most of it than Tupou, whose deeds under the brightest of lights have made him a stone-cold living legend of the club he'll once again try to bring to glory on Sunday.

"It's in the preparation. We've worked so hard during the year to earn this moment," said Tupou.

"It's nothing less than what we've already done, we just have to stay consistent."

title: Union, community say $500k 'woefully inadequate' for Alice Springs College
text:
The Australian Education Union (AEU) says half a million dollars will not be enough to cover all necessary infrastructure upgrades at the new Alice Springs high school merger.

From the start of 2027, Centralian Middle School (CMS) and Centralian Senior College (CSC) will merge to become the Alice Springs College on the current CMS site in Gillen.

The school community has raised concerns that many classrooms, the hall and the library will be too small to fit extra students, while science and computer labs and the home economics kitchen need upgrading.

Brian Gray says $500,000 "does not buy a lot of school". (Supplied: Australian Education Union)

AEU NT branch president Brian Gray said the school needed repainting, had an ineffective air-conditioning system, broken or repeatedly breaking lifts meaning the school was inaccessible and more than the allocated $500,000 was needed for renovations.

"In a climate in which millions have been spent on truancy officers and hundreds of millions to upgrade prisons and build work camps, why has the same financial commitment not been given to invest in the young people of Alice Springs and build them the school they can be proud of and deserve?" Mr Gray said, quoting union members.

"We've had this fantastic announcement of $14 million to build these new sports facilities right next door to the CMS site.

" $14 million buys you a heck of a lot of oval, $500,000 doesn't buy you a lot of school. "

$14.5m NT sports complex The Gillen Oval Multi-Sport Precinct has been green-lit and could become a shop window for Indigenous soccer players, former Manchester United star and Danish international Jesper Olsen says.

He said the school community also wanted certainty around how exactly the $500,000 would be spent and when upgrades would be complete, information which had so far been unclear to staff and families.

'Significant need' for funding

CSC school council chair and a parent of children at both CMS and CSC Rachel Neary said $500,000 was "woefully inadequate", but schools in Palmerston had been provided more than $100 million to update science labs, tech areas and home economic rooms.

"We're not advocating for taking money off schools in Darwin, but actually what we're asking for … is needs-based funding and what we have at the new emerging Alice Springs College is significant need," she said.

Data from the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority shows 60 per cent of students at CMS and 48 per cent of students at CSC were in the bottom quarter for socio-educational advantage, compared to 25 per cent nationally.

"So it's a school where there's a significant amount of need," Ms Neary said.

Rachel Neary says this is an opportunity to expand the school to support central Australian students. (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher)

Mr Gray said there were 1,700 children in public primary schools in Alice Springs and only about 700 in public high schools, so the merger was an opportunity for the NT government to create a school that would keep children in public education.

"Alice Springs College needs to be a school that supports [students] to reach their fullest potential as the future leaders of this town," he said.

Ms Neary said the merger was a once-in-a lifetime opportunity.

"We could really create something significant for young people in Central Australian region," she said.

Money amount uncertain

Department of Education acting deputy chief executive Miranda Watt said more funding would be provided to the Alice Springs College, which would likely be used for updating areas such as science labs and disability access, similar to what was delivered to Driver Secondary School and Rosebury Secondary School in Palmerston.

"[The amount of funding] is yet to be decided, but there's certainly a commitment that that will happen," she said.

Centralian Middle School in Alice Springs will become the new Alice Springs College. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

Ms Watt defended the school's current infrastructure, saying CMS had in previous years had more than 1,000 students, with the only infrastructure changes since then being that some walls had been removed to open up spaces.

"So by putting those additional walls in and updating the spaces to be a little bit more contemporary, it means that many students could attend," she said.

She said while the school's hall may be inadequate for the influx of extra students, there were plenty of other large areas that could be used for assemblies.

Australia’s big four banks are expected to follow Macquarie and pass on the Reserve Bank’s quarter-percentage-point rate rise to home owners, adding $122 in monthly repayments on a standard $800,000 mortgage, and increasing borrowers’ pain following three rate rises earlier this year. Macquarie Bank, the nation’s fifth-largest home lender, said on Tuesday it will pass on the central bank’s 25-basis-point increase in full, with the change taking effect from October 15. Vodafone will let customers pay off a new phone over four years, making it the first Australian telco to offer a 48-month device repayment plan as latest models can cost more than $5000. title: Largest coal mining proposal in state’s history wins approval
text:
The NSW government’s independent planning body has approved the largest coal mining proposal in the state’s history, saying that, while the 800 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions it will cause will have impacts on the Hunter Valley, they can be managed with the conditions it has applied.

In approving the extensions of two sections of the Hunter Valley mining operation for 19 years, known as the HVO extension, the Independent Planning Commission said it had directed the owners – miners Yancoal and Glencore – to export the coal only to countries that had measures in place to limit emissions in line with the goals of the Paris Agreement, and to develop a plan to reduce emissions from the mining operation itself.

The north and south Hunter Valley Operations mines, as seen from above. Google Maps

“The commission finds that the residual impacts of the project are, on balance, outweighed by its benefits to the Hunter region and NSW, including continued employment, economic activity, support for local business, ongoing royalties and taxation revenue.”

Environment groups responded furiously. Georgina Woods, NSW co-ordinator for Lock the Gate, said it was a betrayal of the Hunter Valley community and evidence of institutional failure in a state that is already off-track to meet its own legislated emission reductions of 50 per cent by 2030 and 70 per cent by 2035.

title: WA pollution reports assigned to employees no longer working for watchdog
text:

Breaking NationalWAEnvironmental protection WA pollution reports assigned to employees no longer working for watchdog Holly Thompson September 30, 2026 — 2:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The environmental watchdog failed to adequately track or manage thousands of cases of contamination across Western Australia, often taking years to investigate a site or leaving the responsibility of assessment to staff members that no longer worked there. The WA Auditor General’s scathing report into the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation’s assessment of contaminated sites found over 1200 possibly contaminated sites – out of a total of 1633 – had been awaiting additional assessment information for more than five years with limited follow-up. A site along the swan river was reported as contaminated in 2013. It has still not been investigated. Adobe Stock Acting Auditor General Aloha Morrissey said the department also did not adequately track or manage cases, with 771 sites assigned to staff who no longer worked there at the time of the audit. Of that number, 110 possibly contaminated sites were deemed a high priority, while the department also juggles more than 1500 cases of known contamination.

Advertisement

One of the worst cases uncovered by Morrissey was a formal report to the department back in 2013 on public land close to homes, recreational areas and the Swan River. The pollution watch hotline also received a call reporting an oil spill at the same location. The site was assigned a high-priority rating as heavy metals, hydrocarbons and hazardous chemicals from poor industrial and waste practices were suspected, but since issuing a notification of classification, little has been done to get the information needed to further assess the site. “DWER has not contacted the private operator that leases the land nor any other responsible parties and has never received any updates,” the audit reads. “The staff member currently assigned to this case is no longer employed by DWER. As a result, the level of risk for this site remains uncertain.”

Advertisement

Morrissey said the audit found DWER was not doing enough to get this additional information and progress sites that need further assessment. “For many sites, it is taking DWER years to assess contamination levels as DWER is not maintaining contact with responsible parties,” she said. “The assessment and remediation of contaminated sites can be complex and take years. “Contaminated sites can pose significant threats to public and environmental health and impact future land use.” The audit reviewed a sample of 25 case files for high-priority sites with possible contamination, including the case along the Swan River.

Advertisement

Fourteen had external auditors who provided annual reports to the Department and the remaining 11 relied solely on the department to follow up with the responsible parties. “We found most had limited contact from DWER other than the initial follow up. At nine of the sites, DWER had not contacted the responsible party for over three years,” the report reads. Morrissey said those issues reflected broader weaknesses in the department’s systems. “Several weaknesses found during our audit increase the likelihood of unauthorised access to information, including the confidential identity of people who report potential contamination,” she said. “Of further concern are weak data validation, a lack of system integration and availability risks.”

title: Why you shouldn’t rush to value your property ahead of 2027 tax change
text:

MoneyPlanning & budgetingAsk an expert Opinion Why you shouldn’t rush to value your property ahead of 2027 tax change Noel Whittaker Money columnist Updated September 30, 2026 — 2:09pm , first published September 30, 2026 — 5:00am

Updated September 30, 2026 — 2:09pm ,first published September 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Under the new capital gains tax rules, some properties may need a market value established at June 30, 2027 so that gains accruing before and after July 1, 2027 can be calculated. Given the huge number of properties potentially involved and the relatively small number of valuers, should property owners arrange a valuation before June 30, or will the tax office accept a retrospective valuation done later? We are confused because we have heard two different views. Furthermore, do we need a registered valuer? An Australian Taxation Office spokesman tells me there is no need to rush out and have your property valued before June 30, 2027. In fact, if you intend to rely on a market valuation, you should not obtain one now. A prospective valuation – one prepared before the specified valuation date – will not be acceptable. A retrospective valuation prepared later can be used and, in many cases, may be preferable because the valuer will then have access to a broader range of records and comparable sales around the relevant date, allowing a more informed assessment. The new rules apply to capital gains accruing from July 1, 2027, but tax is generally not payable until the gain is eventually realised. Suzanne White There is another important point. The new rules apply to capital gains accruing from July 1, 2027, but tax is generally not payable until the gain is eventually realised, such as when the property is sold. If you choose to use a valuation-based method to work out your tax consequences, you will only need the valuation, at June 30, when preparing your tax return in the year of disposal and self-assessing your taxable gain. You may, of course, choose to obtain the valuation earlier. Importantly, not every affected property will necessarily need a formal valuation. Taxpayers may have a choice between establishing the property’s market value immediately before 1 July 2027 and using an alternative apportionment method the Government is developing. The Tax Office says it will provide further guidance, tools and calculators once the legislation and method are settled.

Advertisement

As for whether you need a registered or professional valuer, the tax office says that, for tax purposes, the acceptability of a valuation usually depends on the valuation process and the asset being valued rather than simply on who conducted the valuation. There are exceptions – for example, a professional valuer is required for a market valuation for GST margin scheme purposes. The tax office also points out that valuations undertaken by professional valuers are generally more credible than those prepared by somebody who is not a professional valuer. But engaging a professional does not shift the responsibility. The onus remains on the taxpayer to provide a valuation that is replicable and defensible. The tax office says its forthcoming guidance will give more detail on how market values may be determined for different types of CGT assets, the types of professionals taxpayers may wish to engage, and the documents and records that should be kept. The message is simple: don’t panic and don’t pay for a valuation now. Wolter Peeters Meanwhile, the message is simple: don’t panic and don’t pay for a valuation now. If a market valuation is eventually required, it can be prepared retrospectively for June 30. And before spending money on a professional valuation, wait for the tax office’s detailed guidance on exactly what will be required. Under the proposed capital gains tax changes, I understand that if I buy shares now, they will effectively be treated as having been sold on June 30 and repurchased on July 1. Suppose they have risen in value by June 30, but I have owned them for less than 12 months. Does that mean the gain before July 1 will not qualify for the 50 per cent CGT discount and will ultimately be taxed at my marginal rate when the shares are sold? Given the 12-month rule, could there be a case for delaying some share purchases until after June 30?

Advertisement

Technically, there is “deemed disposal” on June 30 and re-acquisition on July 1, however, any capital gain/loss is disregarded and deferred until when the shares are eventually sold. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert Ditch the credit card? Why it’s time to switch to debit Noel Whittaker Money columnist The value at that date will be used to calculate the pre-July 1 component of the capital gain when you eventually dispose of the shares. Provided you have owned the shares for at least 12 months by the time you actually dispose of them, the pre-July 1 component will still qualify for the 50 per cent CGT discount. Therefore, the fact that you may have owned the shares for less than 12 months at June 30 does not, by itself, cause you to lose the discount. I am 70, retired and drawing a flexi pension from my UniSuper balance, currently around $975,000. My wife is 63, also retired, and has about $1.35 million in UniSuper. We have decided to preserve her super for as long as possible and live on mine until it is eventually exhausted. We own our home and have no other significant assets.

Advertisement

Given our ages and super balances, could either of us qualify for the age pension or a part pension? How would Centrelink treat my wife’s super while she is still under the pension age, and what happens once she reaches that age? Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert I’ve inherited $400,000 in shares. What should I do with them? Paul Benson Money contributor Your wife’s super will not count for the asset test until she reaches pensionable age, which is 67, unless she starts to draw a pension from it. Depending on your other assets, you may be eligible for a part pension, provided your total assessable assets do not exceed $1,121,000. If your total assessable assets are a little over the cut-off point, you could seek advice about investing in one of those lifetime income-stream products, where generally only 60 per cent of the purchase price is initially counted for the assets test. This could give you a tiny pension, plus an income stream. But they’re highly specialised, so make sure you understand the product if you decide to choose one. You may also be eligible for the Commonwealth seniors health card, subject to the income test. I’m considering giving both my adult children some money to contribute to super. One is a low-income hospitality worker and the other is a stay-at-home mum. They are in their 30s, and I’m thinking of perhaps $10,000 to $20,000 each. I realise they may have more immediate uses for the money, but I’m also conscious of the power of compounding if the money goes into super at their age. Is contributing to their super a worthwhile strategy, and what contribution and tax issues should we consider?

Advertisement

I understand what you mean about compounding. Putting $10,000 or $20,000 into super in their 30s gives the money decades to grow, but the downside is that it will generally be inaccessible until they reach preservation age, which for both of them will be 60, and satisfy a condition of release. However, if they are likely to buy their first home in the future, consider the First Home Super Saver (FHSS) scheme. You could give them the money and they could then make eligible personal voluntary contributions to their own super. This distinction is important because contributions made directly into their super by a parent are not eligible for the FHSS scheme. They can have up to $15,000 of eligible voluntary contributions in any one financial year count towards the scheme, up to $50,000 across all years, plus associated earnings. Putting $10,000 or $20,000 into a super account when the account-holder is in their 30s gives the money decades to grow. Getty Importantly, if they never buy a home, the money is not lost. It simply remains in super under the normal rules and can generally be accessed from age 60 once they retire or otherwise satisfy a condition of release. So the real question is whether they are better off having the money available now or locking it away for either a first home or retirement. title: Australia's card surcharge ban starts tomorrow. Here's everything you need to know
text:
in brief The surcharge ban covers eftpos, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.

The changes do not affect legitimate booking fees, service fees, delivery charges or hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays.

From tomorrow, the familiar sting of a card surcharge will disappear for Australians paying with most major cards.

But the changes come with a few catches — and not every checkout fee is going away.

Here’s what consumers need to know.

What exactly changes from tomorrow?

From 1 October, businesses can no longer add a separate surcharge simply because a customer pays by card on the affected payment networks.

The change comes through new no-surcharge rules introduced by the card networks and follows a Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) review into card payment costs and surcharging that found removing them would support a more efficient and competitive payments system.

"When card surcharging ends, the sticker price will be the price that consumers end up paying," the RBA website explained.

In other words, if an item is advertised at $100, that's the price you'll pay and you should no longer see an extra card-payment fee added when you tap or insert your card.

Which cards and payment methods are covered?

The surcharge ban covers EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.

American Express and UnionPay are also removing surcharges from 1 October, while PayPal's equivalent change takes effect on 5 October.

The rules generally apply whether the card was issued in Australia or overseas, although individual network rules and exemptions can apply.

Does the ban apply online as well as in-store?

Yes. The change is about the payment method, not whether you are standing at a shop counter or buying from a website.

So an online retailer cannot simply retain a separate Visa, Mastercard or EFTPOS card surcharge because the transaction happens online. The same principle applies to card payments made through apps and other digital checkout systems.

Can businesses still charge booking fees, service fees or weekend surcharges?

Yes, as the RBA site explained: "The changes only apply to surcharges added because a customer pays by card."

The changes do not affect legitimate booking fees, service fees, delivery charges or hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays.

Will this make paying cheaper?

The end of surcharges does not necessarily mean lower prices.

Businesses will still have costs associated with processing card payments, but what's changing is they can no longer add them as an extra fee. They may choose to incorporate them into the total price.

The RBA says, "those costs can be reflected in a business’s overall pricing, rather than charged as a separate surcharge".

Could businesses raise prices instead?

Yes. Businesses are generally free to set and change their prices, as long as they do not mislead customers.

READ MORE How to slash your bills and get money back into your pocket quickly

That means a cafe, retailer, or professional service could increase its standard price to cover payment-processing costs.

Can businesses set minimum spends or stop accepting cards?

Businesses can choose which payment methods they accept and can set minimum card-payment amounts, subject to applicable rules.

So don't assume every business will have to accept your card simply because surcharges are disappearing.

Can businesses offer discounts for paying by cash or another method?

Yes. Businesses can encourage customers to use another payment method by offering a discount rather than imposing a card surcharge.

For example, a business could offer a discount for paying by cash or PayID.

What should you do if you’re still charged a card surcharge?

The consumer watchdog has advice for customers who suspect they've been hit with a card surcharge.

First, check what the fee actually is. It may be a legitimate booking, service or weekend surcharge rather than a card-payment surcharge.

If it appears to be a card surcharge, raise it with the business and ask them to remove the fee or refund it.

"Businesses shouldn’t try to avoid the 'no surcharge' rules … by describing a card payment surcharge as another type of fee or charge," the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said on its website.

From 1 October, consumers can also raise concerns with the relevant card network or the business's payment provider and can report potentially misleading pricing to the ACCC or their state or territory consumer protection agency.

title: How one pensioner's eviction became a flashpoint in Spain's housing crisis
text:
In brief Spain’s government proposed banning evictions until 2030 and curbing property speculation amid a housing crisis.

An 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked protests accepted a deal to return to her home.

Spain's coalition government said it had agreed to proposals including banning evictions until 2030 to address the country's housing crisis, as the 87-year-old woman whose forced removal last week triggered protests accepted an offer to return home.

Hundreds of people remained camped in one of Madrid's main squares on Tuesday to protest Maricarmen Abascal's removal from her home on a stretcher last week. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes.

Spanish health minister Monica Garcia said the ruling Socialists reached an agreement with junior partner Sumar on Tuesday for a set of new measures, including rolling over contracts until 2028 and banning so-called vulture funds from the housing market.

However, the minority government faces an uphill battle to secure support in a fragmented parliament.

The government was seeking to broaden the definition of what constitutes a vulture fund beyond large private equity funds to any fund or company that buys housing for speculation, housing minister Isabel Rodriguez told a news conference, naming Urbagestion, the small company that evicted Abascal, as an example of a firm that might fall into that category.

The measures will be divided into two decrees to be voted on in parliament later this week, with the majority in a first decree. The "final sticking point" of automatic contract rollover is in a second decree, social affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy told a news conference.

'Time to intervene'

"It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," Garcia said in a post on X.

Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing on all measures and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain.

"We all agreed that evictions — where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros — obviously need to be stopped," Junts parliamentary spokesperson Miriam Nogueras said on RTVE.

"Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property — putting them all in the same basket — is a mistake," she added.

Madrid's tenants' union criticised the government's decision to split the measures into two decrees and said the Madrid encampment and others across Spain would continue until their full demands were met, with further demonstrations planned.

The lawyer for pensioner Abascal said on Tuesday that Urbagestion, the fund that owns her apartment, had offered a preliminary agreement that will allow her return to her home, paying 30 per cent of her pension over the next eight years, equivalent to around €500 ($811) a month.

This would see her paying at a similar level to before the eviction.

"She should never have been forced to leave," Beatriz Duro told reporters. "I hope this case serves to provide a collective response to the housing crisis."

title: 'Grading each other's homework': AI industry CEOs bow to Trump-led push for self-regulation
text:
In brief Donald Trump said leading AI companies had signed a "morally binding" pact to self-regulate and improve safeguards.

Tech leaders backed stronger oversight measures, but debate over AI risks and regulation remained unresolved.

United States President Donald Trump says the tech executives who gathered at the White House on Wednesday to discuss regulating AI had signed a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards for the fast-moving technology.

"They're going to police themselves," Trump said after the meeting that gathered the top leaders in artificial intelligence, including Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei.

Trump said the tech bosses had signed a deal that would put on paper their commitment to self-regulate in a morally binding agreement that would not be legally enforceable.

But the final document, dubbed the White House Accord, left the door open "to codify these steps into laws or regulations" if it made sense over time.

Speaking to reporters outside the Oval Office surrounded by the world's most powerful tech bosses, Trump also confirmed that he would officially rename the technology "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence "because it's not artificial".

Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg said the accord aims to assure customers that AI technology "works in the way that we intend".

The commitment includes "robust internal controls" and multiple layers of auditing — from internal risk reviews to external auditors and oversight from the companies' boards of directors, he said.

Zuckerberg called it a starting point for industry-wide standards.

Elon Musk said the executives essentially agreed to "grading each other's homework, which is a lot better than if people just grade their own homework, for obvious reasons".

The lunch meeting also included Amazon's Jeff Bezos, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Sundar Pichai of Google.

READ MORE OpenAI apologises for AI models that breached Australian government websites

Of the 31 guests, two were women: Susie Wiles, Donald Trump's chief of staff, and Lisa Su, CEO of semiconductor company AMD.

The gathering occurred as attitudes toward AI sour in Washington DC, with politicians increasingly under pressure from voters to curb or slow AI development over fears it could displace workers and upend society.

Those concerns gained force from a run of incidents in which OpenAI's autonomous systems slipped out of their constraints, starting with a July breach of Hugging Face — a widely used platform for sharing AI models.

OpenAI announced on Tuesday that it was cancelling the release of its latest model, known as Astra 6.1, after internal testing by the ChatGPT-maker revealed it did not meet safety standards.

Trump, advised by Huang and his former AI czar David Sacks, has urged unfettered AI development to outpace China and fuel a US economy increasingly dependent on AI-driven growth.

The issue of data centres, the vast computing facilities the technology requires, has emerged as a flashpoint in midterm election races in both parties, with more and more communities worried about rising electricity bills and the strain on water and land.

Trump has dismissed opponents of these data centres and, after the meeting, insisted that AI companies "will be very generous" with communities who open their doors to them.

"They'll help with their schools, they'll help with their teachers," he said.

'Still under discussion'

Major AI companies, particularly Anthropic and OpenAI, have issued stark public warnings about uncontrolled development of increasingly powerful systems — even as they develop and deploy this same state-of-the-art technology.

Those concerns intensified after a former employee of both companies went public with warnings that the industry is moving faster than safety reviews allow.

Anthropic warned investors of potential existential risks to humanity in the prospectus for its highly anticipated initial public offering, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.

Anthropic is aiming for an IPO as early as November.

Trump has repeatedly characterised these warnings about existential risks as overblown, and the White House has bitterly clashed with Anthropic over AI safety.

"As the president has said, whoever wins AI, wins. I think that's very important," Amodei said after the meeting. "But I think the technology has very real risks, and the mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion."

title: Socceroos shine bright and fizzle out in action-packed clash with Brazil in Brisbane
text:
In brief The Socceroos went down 4-2 to Brazil in their second friendly match.

After a muscular first half that rattled Brazil's cage, the Australian defence couldn't hold the visitors at bay.

A fired-up Brazil team has outgunned the Socceroos 4-2 in a dramatic rematch in which the hosts held a brief lead thanks to a Connor Metcalfe stunner.

A 1-1 draw in Townsville on Friday clearly stirred five-time World Cup champions Brazil.

The Brazilians scored in the third minute on Tuesday and, after a fiery tussle that spilled onto the Socceroos' bench, found two late goals to secure victory in front of a sell-out 52,423-strong Lang Park crowd.

Australia led until the final play in Townsville and will leave Brisbane frustrated after again throwing away good chances to notch a famous victory.

title: Australia is closing in on the world's highest rates. Only one country is in front
text:
IN BRIEF Australia's cash rate is now one of the highest in the world, but lower than Iceland's.

Experts say Iceland's dramatic rate is the product of over two decades of financial instability.

Australia has the second-highest interest rate among comparable economies after the Reserve Bank hiked rates to a 15-year high on Tuesday.

Taking the crown is Iceland, where the cash rate currently sits at 8 per cent — the highest of the 41 advanced economies as defined by the International Monetary Fund.

The Central Bank of Iceland set the historic rate in August, claiming the increase was "driven mainly by hikes in public levies and price increases caused by the war in the Middle East".

Similarly, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) cited higher energy and fuel prices and the Middle East conflict as reasons for Australia's hike from 4.35 per cent to 4.6 per cent.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers denied a fair comparison could be made between Australia and Iceland's interest rates.
